notes: ASBO breach sentence appeal; prior Court of Appeal guidance on ASBO sentencing and public protection analysis are clear.

enrichment.short_title: ASBO breach sentence appeal after early release
key_facts: Braxton was subject to a Birmingham City Centre ASBO prohibiting threatening, abusive or violent behaviour for five years from October 2001.
He was previously convicted of two ASBO breaches and sentenced to four years, reduced on appeal to two years; he was released on licence in April 2003.
Within weeks of release he again breached the ASBO by aggressive begging and slapping a woman, and assaulted a constable by spitting in his face.
Committed for sentence in the Crown Court, he received three and a half years on each breach concurrent plus three months consecutive for the assault.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for leave to appeal against sentence following refusal by the single judge.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; sentence upheld as necessary to protect the public from persistent ASBO breaches.
enrichment.ratio: Breaches of antisocial behaviour orders must reflect Parliament's concern about repeated antisocial conduct; where an offender has already received a substantial sentence for earlier breaches and quickly reoffends on release, a further substantial custodial term may be justified to protect the public even if individual incidents appear at the lower end of nuisance activity.
legal_issues: Whether the Crown Court sentence for second ASBO breaches was manifestly excessive
Whether begging and minor assaults should be treated as lower-end nuisance conduct
Whether alleged defects in magistrates' summary trial procedure could be raised on sentence appeal
Application of prior Court of Appeal guidance on maximum ASBO breach sentences
linked_authorities: R v Braxton [2003] EWCA Crim (earlier ASBO sentence appeal)

confidence.notes: Sentence reasoning, ASBO history and outcome are explicit. Conviction challenge points were correctly held unavailable in the Court of Appeal.

notes: Interlocutory ruling only; stay of costs enforcement lifted and modest litigant-in-person costs awarded to second defendant.

enrichment.short_title: Medtia v Hamid: stay lifted and preliminary costs
key_facts: Medtia appealed against a County Court judgment in favour of Dr Hamid in a builder-client dispute also involving second defendant Richard Clare.
Clare appeared at the appeal hearing although only Hamid's judgment was under appeal; County Court costs in his favour had been stayed pending the appeal.
The Court of Appeal held the stay on enforcement of Clare's costs certificate could no longer stand once the appeal proceeded.
Clare claimed £2,730 for 40 hours at an architect's rate of £65 per hour; the court awarded £350 including rail fare.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Preliminary application at the start of a civil appeal concerning stay of costs and costs of the hearing day.
enrichment.outcome: Stay of enforcement of Clare's costs certificate discharged; costs of the preliminary hearing awarded to second defendant in the sum of £350.
enrichment.ratio: A stay of costs enforcement pending appeal cannot continue once the appeal is being heard; a litigant in person who attends unnecessarily without enquiry may recover only modest costs proportionate to the day's attendance rather than extensive preparation time.
legal_issues: Whether a stay of costs enforcement should remain in force during the appeal
Whether the second defendant was entitled to costs of attending the appeal hearing
Assessment of reasonable costs for a litigant in person appearing on a preliminary point

confidence.notes: Interlocutory orders are clear though the substantive appeal merits were not decided in this judgment.

notes: Special measures screens under YJCEA 1999 section 17 and aggravated burglary sentence appeal; judge's discretion upheld.

enrichment.short_title: Aggravated burglary: screens direction and sentence

statutes_considered.title: Youth Justice and Criminal Evidence Act 1999

key_facts: Brown and Grant were convicted of aggravated burglary after entering a flat at about 1.30 am armed with a knife and hammer seeking Steventon brothers.
The prosecution case was joint entry as trespassers intending grievous bodily harm; the defence said weapons were for protection against a dog.
Witnesses Adela, Warren and Leigh Steventon gave evidence from behind screens under section 17 YJCEA 1999; Walji did not.
Brown was sentenced to four years and Grant to five years' imprisonment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeals against conviction and, for Brown, against sentence following trial at Blackfriars Crown Court.
enrichment.outcome: Conviction appeals dismissed; Brown's sentence appeal dismissed; late special measures application and jury direction on screens upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Section 17(2)(a) permits screens where witness quality is likely to be diminished by fear or distress because of the nature and circumstances of the offence; late applications for screens are directory rather than mandatory under the Special Measures Directions Rules, and a clear direction given before witnesses give evidence need not be repeated in the summing-up if the jury are effectively warned.
legal_issues: Whether witnesses should have been permitted to give evidence behind screens
Whether late special measures applications complied with rule 4(2)(b)
Whether the jury required a repeated screens warning in the summing-up
Whether Brown's four-year sentence for aggravated burglary was excessive
linked_authorities: R v Daniel [2000] 2 Cr App R(S) 184

confidence.notes: Special measures reasoning and sentence analysis are detailed and the appeals outcome is explicit.

notes: Reserved judgment on similar-fact joinder and section 23/26 hearsay admission; Article 6 analysis thorough though fact-specific.

enrichment.short_title: Double wounding: similar fact and hearsay witness
key_facts: Arnold was convicted of two section 18 wounding-with-intent offences after unprovoked slashings outside Croydon pubs on the same evening in December 2001.
Witness Daley Stevens identified Arnold in a police statement but later retracted and refused to attend trial; the statement was read under section 23 CJA 1988.
Christopher Morley identified Arnold at parade for the second attack; fingerprint evidence placed Arnold at the first pub.
The Crown relied on similar fact evidence linking the two motiveless face-and-body slashings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction with leave of the single judge; reserved reasons after oral dismissal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; severance refused, similar fact evidence admissible, and Stevens' hearsay statement properly admitted under section 26 discretion.
enrichment.ratio: Two proximate, motiveless slash attacks outside pubs with comparable facial and abdominal injuries may satisfy the DPP v P / R v W similar-fact test for identity; where a frightened witness resiles from an identification statement, section 26 requires careful scrutiny but admission may be justified when similar fact evidence means the statement is not sole or determinative and ample material exists to controvert it consistently with Article 6.
legal_issues: Whether the two counts should have been severed
Admissibility of similar fact evidence on identity
Admissibility of injury photographs without medical causation evidence
Whether Stevens' witness statement should have been read under sections 23 and 26
Article 6 fairness where absent witness provides identification evidence

R v W (John) [1998] 2 Cr App Rep 289
R v Dragic [1996] 2 Cr App Rep 232
R v M (KJ) [2003] EWCA Crim 357
Luca v Italy (2003) 36 EHRR 46
Regina v Blackstock 70 Cr App Rep 34

notes: CCRC referral; clear PACE section 58 breach and Crown concession that excluded confessions left no safe case to answer.

enrichment.short_title: 1986 murder conviction quashed for PACE section 58 breach
key_facts: James was convicted in 1986 of murder and conspiracy to rob after Charles Pelham was shot during an attempted robbery at a travelling showmen's caravan site.
Key prosecution evidence comprised police interview admissions and a written statement made while James was denied access to a solicitor over seven hours on 17 January 1986.
The Criminal Cases Review Commission referred the case because of PACE section 58 breaches shortly after the Act came into force.
The Crown conceded the interviews should have been excluded and that without them there was no safe case to answer.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal following CCRC reference against 1986 murder and conspiracy convictions previously refused leave.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; murder and conspiracy convictions quashed as unsafe.
enrichment.ratio: Denial of access to a solicitor during critical interviews in breach of PACE section 58, where the superintendent did not apply the strict 'will lead' test later explained in R v Samuel and could not reasonably have believed a duty solicitor would alert suspects or hinder recovery of evidence, renders resulting confessions inadmissible; if excluded, corroborated co-accused evidence alone could not safely sustain conviction.
legal_issues: Whether confessions obtained without solicitor access should have been excluded under sections 76 or 78 PACE
Correct interpretation of section 58 delay provisions and Code C
Effect of excluding confessions on safety of murder and conspiracy convictions
Retrospective application of post-1986 Court of Appeal guidance to early PACE cases
linked_authorities: R v Samuel (1988) 87 Cr App R 232
R v Allerdice (1988) 87 Cr App R 380
R v Absolam 88 Cr App R 332
R v Roberts (19.3.98)

confidence.notes: Crown concession and section 58 analysis are explicit; conviction quashed on conceded unsafe basis.

notes: Majority conviction for indecent assault on child; no case to answer submission and identification evidence analysis clear.

enrichment.short_title: Hospital indecent assault: identification no case to answer
key_facts: McConnell, a secure-unit in-patient, was convicted by majority verdict of indecently assaulting nine-year-old Daniel in a hospital garden at Cheddleton in June 2001.
Daniel gave video-recorded evidence; he gave no detailed description at interview and there was over a year before the video identification parade.
Daniel said his mother pointed out the appellant in the canteen before the parade, though the mother denied this.
Supporting evidence included the mother and a nurse seeing McConnell leaving the area hurriedly and appearing scared.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction by leave of the single judge following trial at Stoke-on-Trent Crown Court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; judge properly rejected no case to answer submission and left identification to the jury.
enrichment.ratio: Weak identification evidence from a child complainant does not require acquittal at the close of the prosecution case where undisputed assault is corroborated by witnesses who knew the defendant placing him leaving the scene hurriedly shortly afterwards; it is for a properly directed jury to assess overall identification reliability.
legal_issues: Whether identification evidence was too weak to leave to the jury
Effect of delay and prior canteen pointing-out on identification reliability
Whether no case to answer submission should have succeeded
Corroboration from mother, partner and psychiatric nurse

confidence.notes: Identification weaknesses and corroborative evidence are fully analysed; summing-up accepted as fair.

notes: Builder-client Scott Schedule arithmetic errors and global counterclaim award overturned; detailed quantum recalculation.

enrichment.short_title: Medtia v Hamid: building defects quantum appeal
key_facts: Medtia, a builder, and Dr Hamid fell out over defective renovation works at Hamid's home; a six-day County Court trial before Recorder Fordham QC produced confused judgments.
The recorder made arithmetical errors including double-counting the counterclaim and misreading the Scott Schedule allowed/reduction columns.
Hamid's additional counterclaim items totalling over £8,000 were allowed only as a global £2,500 despite limited evidence.
The Court of Appeal recalculated quantum and substituted judgment for the claimant of about £2,238 after correcting the Scott Schedule and removing the global award.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against revised County Court judgment awarding Dr Hamid £6,898.75 on building contract and counterclaim dispute.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; judgment for claimant substituted in the recalculated sum of approximately £2,238; interest refused.
enrichment.ratio: A Scott Schedule requires point-by-point adjudication of defects and remedial costs; a judge cannot substitute a global counterclaim award without itemised findings, and fundamental arithmetical errors in treating allowed figures as reductions or double-counting counterclaims require appellate correction regardless of general impressions about workmanship.
legal_issues: Correct construction of Scott Schedule allowed and reduction columns
Whether global award of £2,500 for additional counterclaim items was justified
Double counting of counterclaim in revised judgment arithmetic
Whether duplicate item 73 roofing deduction should stand after rejecting item 2(b)
Entitlement to interest after successful appeal

confidence.notes: Arithmetic corrections and Scott Schedule reasoning are explicit though some item-by-item fact findings remain trial-court territory.

notes: Case stated on no case to answer at close of prosecution case; PACE Code D and section 78 timing in magistrates' courts explained.

enrichment.short_title: Juvenile robbery: no case to answer case stated

statutes_considered.title: Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 Code D

key_facts: Two juveniles, B and J, were charged with robbery of Adam Khaffaf's sovereign ring after an alleyway incident in March 2002.
About four hours later, at Haymill Close, Khaffaf identified the appellants to police who had attended a separate disturbance.
No identification parade was held; Khaffaf's account of how identification occurred conflicted with the officers' evidence.
Magistrates deferred final section 78 ruling but found a case to answer based on Khaffaf's identification evidence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by case stated from Youth Magistrates' Court on whether there was a case to answer at the close of the prosecution case.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; magistrates could properly find a case to answer on the identification evidence heard.
enrichment.ratio: In magistrates' courts section 78 applications need not be determined before evidence is heard and may be deferred; at the close of the prosecution case justices apply the Galbraith test and may find a case to answer where identification evidence, despite Code D breaches or police involvement, is not so manifestly unreliable that no reasonable tribunal could convict.
legal_issues: Timing of section 78 applications in magistrates' courts
Effect of failure to hold an identification parade under Code D
Whether street identification after police suggestion was unsafe
Interaction between section 78 application and no case to answer submission
Whether defendants' later admission of presence affected the submission

notes: Leading section 55 NIAA 2002 asylum support test case; collective Article 3 impact of destitution policy analysed at length.

enrichment.short_title: Asylum support section 55 and Article 3 destitution
key_facts: Conjoined appeals by the Secretary of State against judicial review victories for asylum seekers Limbuela, Tesema and Adam denied support under section 55 NIAA 2002.
Section 55(1) bars destitute support where asylum was not claimed as soon as reasonably practicable; section 55(5) preserves support necessary to avoid Convention breaches.
Limbuela slept rough without food for two nights after eviction before charities and interim relief intervened; hundreds of similar cases awaited guidance.
Evidence showed limited charitable shelter and food capacity if large numbers of refused asylum seekers were left destitute and unable to work.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Secretary of State's appeals against High Court judicial review judgments granting asylum support to destitute late-claiming asylum seekers.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals dismissed; refusal of support under section 55 where it would leave asylum seekers destitute on the streets is unlawful as violating Article 3 individually and collectively.
enrichment.ratio: Section 55(5) requires support where withholding section 95 assistance would expose an asylum seeker to inhuman or degrading treatment; where collective application of the policy will inevitably push a substantial number of destitute, workless asylum seekers below the Article 3 threshold for lack of food and shelter, the policy is unlawful even if no single claimant's case alone proves severity.
legal_issues: Application of section 55(5) NIAA 2002 to avoid Article 3 breaches
Article 3 threshold for destitute asylum seekers denied support and work
Whether R(Q) and R(T) preclude collective unlawfulness findings
Availability of charitable food and shelter provision
General guidance for hundreds of pending section 55 cases

R (T) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] 7 CCLR 53
Zardasht v Secretary of State [2004] EWHC Admin 91

notes: Etridge undue influence principles applied to elderly transfer at undervalue via attorney; transaction set aside with mortgagee directions reserved.

enrichment.short_title: Elderly house transfer set aside for undue influence
key_facts: Mr Vale, a 78-year-old widower, transferred his Lenham home worth about £88,000 to great-nephew Jason for £43,000 mortgage takeover plus an oral life occupation promise.
Terence Armstrong, Mr Vale's attorney, arranged the sale after Mrs Vale's death when Mr Vale feared repossession, though housing benefit covered nearly all mortgage interest.
Jason obtained Halifax and Birmingham Midshires mortgages using false statements that the property would be vacant; benefits agencies were misled about rent.
Independent solicitor advice from Mr Duce was inadequate and Mr Vale lacked capacity fully to assess the transaction's security.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Chancery claim to set aside transfer of registered property procured through an enduring power of attorney.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded; transfer voidable for undue influence and to be set aside; consequences for Birmingham Midshires mortgagees reserved for further hearing.
enrichment.ratio: Where a vulnerable elderly transferor reposes trust in a relative attorney and transfers his only substantial asset at a manifest undervalue for an insecure oral right to remain, the Etridge presumption of undue influence arises and is not rebutted by inadequate independent advice or the donor's initial proposal; an attorney who procures such a transfer breaches fiduciary and EPA section 3 duties.
legal_issues: Presumption of undue influence under Royal Bank of Scotland v Etridge (No 2)
Whether transaction was manifestly disadvantageous to Mr Vale
Sufficiency of independent legal advice to rebut presumption
Security of oral right to occupy against mortgagees
Breach of Enduring Powers of Attorney Act 1985 section 3 by attorney
Constructive trust and setting aside registered transfers
linked_authorities: Royal Bank of Scotland plc v Etridge (No 2) [2002] 2 AC 773
CIBC Mortgages Plc v Pitt [1994] 1 AC 200
Cheese v Thomas [1994] 1 WLR 129

confidence.notes: Undue influence findings and Etridge application are detailed; final relief against mortgagees left for further submissions.
